description: A team of students trying to win, sponsored by Furim Institute.
summary:
Mountain rivers in the Alps and Norway drive turbines, cool power plants and supply drinking water. Is that water now arriving in different amounts, or at a different time of year?

RivaScope answers this one river at a time. Pick a river on the map and it shows decades of measured flow: how much water came, when it came, and whether the change is statistically significant or just noise. It covers 117 mountain catchments in Switzerland and Norway and sets the gauge records beside NASA's GLDAS model.

In our Swiss network, July flow is trending down at 97 of 100 gauges.

Users choose their occupation, such as hydropower or data-centre cooling, and see the numbers that matter to it first. Anyone planning around a river can check its record before they commit.
details:
RivaScope is a map-first tool for exploring how mountain river flow has changed. You pick a country and a gauged river on a satellite map and see its measured history: how much water flows, when in the year it arrives, and how low the low flows get.

A Python pipeline reads daily discharge from CAMELS-CH and Norway's NVE for 33 Swiss and 84 Norwegian catchments. It tests each measure for a trend using Sen's slope and a Mann-Kendall test, corrected for autocorrelation and for testing many gauges. The same analysis runs on NASA's GLDAS-2.1 model for comparison.

Users choose an occupation, such as hydropower or data-centre cooling, and see its relevant indicators first. They can enter a flow threshold and see how often the record fell below it. The aim is better-informed questions before anyone plans around a river.

We built it with Python (pandas, SciPy, Plotly), plain JavaScript and Leaflet. Claude Code, OpenAI Codex and Perplexity assisted with the code.

The creative part of it is breaking down the water availability problematic into pieces for better understanding and trending, while also offering a custom risk analysis (e.g. for volatility) per audience occupation, while also backing it up by quantitative arguments.


RivaScope is a historical prototype and does not forecast, although allowing to motivate for precautions.
